items.title: Plain English: choosing the best version in context (Level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK Style Guide; GOV.UK content design guidance
items.body: Plain English is not a list of banned words. It is a way of choosing words and structure that suit the reader and the purpose. A good writer asks three questions: what does the reader need, what must they do, and what is the simplest way to say it accurately? Sometimes a longer sentence is clearer than a short one. 'You can claim if you are 18 or over and live in England' is better than two clipped fragments that leave the link between them unclear. Sometimes a technical word is correct and necessary, such as 'appeal' in a decision letter or 'National Insurance number' on a form. Use it consistently. If you call something a 'claim' in one paragraph, do not call it an 'application' in the next, because readers may think there are two different things. Keep the same word for the same idea. Put conditions before the action when they matter: 'If you miss the deadline, you can still ask us to look again' is easier to follow than a sentence that buries the condition in the middle. Be careful that shorter does not mean less accurate. Do not cut a word such as 'only', 'not' or 'unless' that changes the meaning. Check whether a rewrite has dropped a deadline, a condition or a number. Lastly, remember that plain English does not mean being casual. A letter to a member of the public should be polite and respectful, using 'please' and 'thank you' where they fit, but without stiff or old-fashioned phrases.

questions.prompt: A letter calls a request a 'claim' in paragraph one, an 'application' in paragraph two and a 'submission' in paragraph three. What is the main problem?

options.text: The words are Latin abbreviations most readers do not know
The words are all written in the passive voice
The reader may think these are three different things
The words are too long for a plain English letter to use

questions.hint: Using one word for one idea avoids confusion.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of 'You can claim if you are 18 or over. You live in England.' keeps the link between the two conditions clear?

options.text: Claims are open to over-18s, plus England residents only.
You can claim. You must be 18 or over. You live in England.
You can claim if you are 18 or over and you live in England.
You can claim, 18 or over, living in England.

questions.hint: A joined sentence shows that both conditions must be met.

questions.prompt: Which version puts the condition where it is easiest to follow?

options.text: You can, in the event of a missed deadline, still ask us to look again.
Asking us to look again is possible, where you have missed the deadline.
If you miss the deadline, you can still ask us to look again.
You can still ask us to look again, which is the case if you miss the deadline.

questions.hint: Putting 'if' first tells the reader the condition before the action.

questions.prompt: A writer shortens 'You will only be paid if you return the form' to 'You will be paid if you return the form'. What has gone wrong?

options.text: The sentence is now in the passive voice
The meaning has changed because 'only' has been removed
The sentence is now too long
The sentence now contains a double negative

questions.hint: Words such as 'only' and 'unless' carry meaning and cannot be cut.

questions.prompt: Which statement about technical words in a decision letter is correct?

options.text: Leave technical words out, even if the reader needs them to act on it
Use a different technical word each time to avoid repetition
Replace every technical word with a casual phrase of your own
Use a necessary technical word such as 'appeal' and use it consistently

questions.hint: Necessary terms should be kept and used consistently.

questions.prompt: Which opening is plain but also polite for a first letter to a member of the public?

options.text: Your letter has been received. The decision is as follows.
I refer to your recent correspondence and write to advise of the outcome.
Hey, thanks for getting in touch. Here is what we have decided.
Thank you for your letter of 3 March. I am writing to tell you our decision.

questions.hint: Plain English can be polite and warm without being casual.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of a sentence has dropped a vital detail? Original: 'Send your form by 5 May to the address on page 2.'

options.text: Send your form by 5 May to the address on page 2.
Send your form to the address on page 2.
Please send the form to the address on page 2 by 5 May.
By 5 May, send your form to the address on page 2.

questions.hint: The first option has lost the deadline.

questions.prompt: A draft says 'The department aims to provide a response within 10 working days.' Why might 'We will reply within 10 working days' be better?

options.text: It speaks directly and commits to a clear time
It removes the need for a deadline to be given at all
It uses the passive voice, which sounds more formal
It is longer and so it gives the reader more detail

questions.hint: Direct wording with a clear time helps the reader.

questions.prompt: Which approach is best when a plain English version would be less accurate than the legal wording?

options.text: Use the legal wording and give no explanation of it at all
Use the plain version even if it slightly changes the meaning
Leave out the legal detail so that the sentence stays short
Keep the accurate meaning and explain the legal term in plain words

questions.hint: Accuracy comes first, and explanations help readers.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is plain English but too casual for a letter to a member of the public?

options.text: I'm sorry about the mix-up. I will put it right by Friday.
I apologise for the error. I will correct it by Friday.
We're sorry about the mix-up, and we'll sort it out ASAP, okay?
We are sorry about the mix-up. We will put it right by Friday.

questions.hint: Plain English should still be polite and professional.

items.title: Writing summaries, briefings and longer documents (Level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service writing guidance
items.body: In an office job you will often write notes, summaries or short briefings for a manager who has little time. Begin with the conclusion or recommendation, and then give the evidence. A good summary answers four questions: what is the issue, what do we know, what do we recommend and what is needed from the reader? State clearly if you need a decision by a certain date. Keep to one page where possible. Use headings and short sections so that a busy person can find what they want. Put background in a separate section or an annex, not before the main message. Where you compare options, a small table can be clearer than paragraphs. Make sure numbers are checked and add the source and date for key figures, for example 'Figures are from the claims database on 3 March'. Separate facts from opinions and label opinions as such: 'We think' or 'I recommend'. Do not hide uncertainty. If you do not yet know something, say so and say when you will find out. Do not use unexplained acronyms. If you write an acronym such as DWP, spell it out on first use. When a document goes through several drafts, number the versions and keep track of who has changed what. Finally, proofread. Read once for sense, then again for spelling, numbers, names and dates. Typos in a briefing lower trust in the facts.

questions.prompt: Where should the recommendation go in a briefing for a busy manager?

options.text: In an annex at the back
At the end, after all the background
At the start, before the evidence
Only in the covering email

questions.hint: Starting with the conclusion saves the reader time.

questions.prompt: Which question does a good summary NOT need to answer?

options.text: What is needed from the reader
Who else has read the document
What do we recommend
What is the issue

questions.hint: A summary covers the issue, evidence, recommendation and required action.

questions.prompt: Why add a source and date to a key figure?

options.text: So the reader can judge how reliable and current it is
So the figure takes up more space on the page of the briefing
So the figure can be hidden in an annex at the back of it
So the figure can be changed later without anybody noticing

questions.hint: Sources and dates help readers trust and check figures.

questions.prompt: A briefing compares three options on cost, time and risk. Which format is likely to be clearest?

options.text: A small table with a row for each option
A single long paragraph
A chart without any labels
A bulleted list of the options with no details

questions.hint: A table compares options side by side.

questions.prompt: Which statement is clearly an opinion and labelled as such?

options.text: The deadline appears in the letter.
I recommend that we extend the deadline by two weeks.
The deadline was extended last year.
The deadline is two weeks from today.

questions.hint: Phrases such as 'I recommend' show a view rather than a fact.

questions.prompt: You do not yet know the cost. What is the best way to handle this in a briefing?

options.text: Leave the cost out so the briefing looks complete
Repeat last year's cost without comment
Say it is not yet known and give a date for when it will be
Give an estimate without saying it is an estimate

questions.hint: Honesty about uncertainty builds trust.

questions.prompt: Why should background information go in a separate section or annex?

options.text: So the main message can be left unwritten
So the briefing looks longer
So the reader cannot find the background
So the main message is not buried

questions.hint: Busy readers want the main point first.

questions.prompt: Why is it good practice to number the versions of a draft document?

options.text: Everyone can tell which version is the latest
The number replaces the title
The document will be read more quickly
Earlier versions can be deleted without a record

questions.hint: Version numbers prevent confusion between drafts.

questions.prompt: Which proofreading approach is most effective?

options.text: Run a spell check and send it to your manager at once
Ask the person who wrote the figures to read it for you
Read it once quickly, immediately after you have finished writing
Read once for sense and again for spelling, numbers, names and dates

questions.hint: Separate passes for sense and detail find more errors.

items.title: Clear dates, numbers and units (Level 4)
items.body: Mistakes about dates and numbers cause real harm, because people may miss a deadline or pay the wrong amount. A date such as 02/03/2025 can mean 2 March in the UK and 3 February in the United States, so always write the month in words: 2 March 2025. Be careful with phrases such as 'next Friday', 'this weekend', 'fortnightly', 'bi-monthly' and 'biannual', because different people read them differently. Use exact dates and 'every two weeks' instead of 'fortnightly'. The word 'between' can be unclear about whether the end dates are included. 'You can apply from 1 April to 30 April' is clearer. 'By 5 May' means on or before 5 May, whereas 'before 5 May' means up to and not including 5 May. State the time when it matters, such as 'by 5pm on 5 May'. Write large numbers in full with commas in figures, such as 1,500,000, and use 'million' in text, for example '1.5 million'. Round only where it will not mislead, and say so. Give units with every measurement: £, kg, days. Say whether a figure includes VAT or is before tax. Write telephone numbers in a consistent way, such as 0300 123 4567. For percentages, make clear what they are a percentage of: 'a 10% rise' could mean a rise of 10 percentage points or 10% of the previous value. Where possible give the actual numbers as well.

questions.prompt: Why is the date 02/03/2025 risky in a letter?

options.text: It uses too many digits for a reader to take in
It uses the wrong year for most government letters
It can be read as 2 March or 3 February
It cannot be read properly by screen readers at all

questions.hint: Writing the month in words prevents misreading.

questions.prompt: Which is clearest for an application window?

options.text: You can apply from 1 April to 30 April.
Applications run through April, give or take.
You can apply between April and the end of the month.
You can apply in April, and not after.

questions.hint: Exact start and end dates remove doubt.

questions.prompt: What does 'by 5 May' mean?

options.text: Exactly on 5 May only
On or before 5 May
After 5 May
Before 5 May, not including the day

questions.hint: 'By' includes the date itself.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid writing 'fortnightly' in a letter to the public?

options.text: It is always misspelt by people who write it
It is a Latin word that most readers will not know
Some readers may not know it means every two weeks
It means every month for some people and every week for others

questions.hint: Plain wording such as 'every two weeks' is clearer.

questions.prompt: Why add 'by 5pm' to a deadline of 5 May?

options.text: It makes the sentence longer and so more formal
It is a legal requirement for all letters sent by departments
It means the real deadline is the day before
It makes clear the time limit on the last day

questions.hint: A time removes uncertainty about the last day.

questions.prompt: A payment is described as '£120'. What else should the reader be told if it matters?

options.text: Which pen or ink the writer used to sign the letter
The day of the week on which the letter was written
The number of the letter within the batch sent that day
Whether it is before or after tax or VAT

questions.hint: Amounts can differ depending on tax.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to write one and a half million in text?

options.text: 1.5 million
one point five million

questions.hint: GOV.UK style uses figures with 'million'.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good practice for telephone numbers?

options.text: Write them in a different format in every document you produce
Write them without spaces to save room on the page
Hide the dialling code so that numbers look shorter
Write them the same way each time, with spaces, such as 0300 123 4567

questions.hint: Consistent spacing helps readers dial correctly.

items.title: Emails in tricky situations (Level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body: Some emails are harder to write than others. When you chase someone who has not replied, be polite and specific. Say what you need, why it matters and by when, and make it easy to reply: 'Could you confirm your address by Friday 14 March so we can send your payment?' Avoid sounding annoyed. When you must say no, give a short reason, offer an alternative if you can, and keep a warm tone: 'I cannot approve this, because it is outside the scheme rules. You could apply for X instead.' If you disagree with a colleague, say so respectfully and give your reasons, and keep to the issue rather than the person. Avoid writing to a colleague in a way you would not want read out in a meeting. Do not copy in someone's manager to put pressure on them, unless you have a good reason and have said so. If an email is too complicated to explain, a short phone call may be better, followed by a note confirming what you agreed. Do not use email to deliver upsetting news to a colleague in the first instance. Use the Civil Service values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Do not reply to emails in anger. Give yourself time. Check the full list of recipients. If you make a mistake, correct it quickly and openly: 'I sent you the wrong date. The correct date is 21 March. I am sorry for any confusion.' Use delegates and out-of-office messages sensibly, so that urgent matters still reach someone.

questions.prompt: Which message is the best way to chase a customer who has not replied?

options.text: I have not heard back from you since my last email. Please reply as soon as possible.
Could you confirm your address by Friday 14 March so we can send your payment?
Why have you not answered my last email?
This is a reminder that you still have not responded.

questions.hint: A polite, specific chaser says what, why and by when.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible response to a colleague whose email you strongly disagree with?

options.text: Reply immediately with a short, sharp message of your own
Say you see it differently, give your reasons and keep to the issue
Copy in their manager so that everybody can see your point
Ignore the email and hope that they eventually forget about it

questions.hint: Respectful, reasoned disagreement keeps working relationships healthy.

questions.prompt: When might a phone call be better than an email?

options.text: When you want to keep a written record of the discussion only
When the topic is complicated or upsetting
When the recipient is on leave for the next two weeks
When the message is only one line long and not urgent

questions.hint: A call lets you explain and respond to reactions.

questions.prompt: What should you do after agreeing something on a call?

options.text: Wait for the other person to write it up and send it round
Send a short note confirming what was agreed
Save a draft of it and look at it again next week
Assume that everyone will remember what was agreed

questions.hint: A written note creates a record.

questions.prompt: You sent a customer the wrong date. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ask a colleague to phone and say it was a typing error
Send a new email without mentioning the mistake
Correct it quickly, give the right date and apologise
Wait to see whether they notice

questions.hint: Quick, open corrections limit confusion.

questions.prompt: Which is a reason not to copy a colleague's manager into an email?

options.text: It makes the email too long for the recipient to read
It can look like an attempt to put pressure on them
It is not possible to copy managers on government systems
Managers do not read any of the emails they are copied into

questions.hint: Copying managers can feel like escalation.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service value is shown by correcting your own mistake openly?

options.text: Loyalty
Impartiality
Speed
Honesty

questions.hint: The Civil Service values are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality.

questions.prompt: Why set an out-of-office message with a colleague's contact details?

options.text: So that the named colleague can read all of your emails
So that you avoid replying to emails when you return
So the sender knows exactly why you are away from work
So urgent matters still reach someone while you are away

questions.hint: A named contact keeps work moving.

items.title: Handling complaints and difficult letters (Level 4)
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Civil Service Code; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman guidance
items.body: A complaint is a chance to put things right and learn. Reply promptly, and acknowledge the complaint straight away, saying when you will give a full reply. Read the complaint closely and list each point the person has raised, and make sure you answer every one. Use the person's own words where you can, so they know you listened. If the department has made a mistake, say so plainly and apologise. If it has not, explain what happened and why, without being defensive. Do not use phrases such as 'we regret that you feel' because they sound as if the problem is the person's feelings. Say what you will do to put things right, such as correct a record, make a payment or change a process. Do not promise what you cannot deliver. Give a named contact. Tell the person what to do if they are still unhappy. Many departments have a multi-stage complaints process, and in the end a person can ask their MP to refer their complaint to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman, which looks into complaints about government departments and the NHS in England. Keep a clear record of the complaint, your reply and any actions. Treat the complaint as a request for help, not an attack, and look at the facts. Never take the complaint personally and never respond in anger, even when the language is rude. If a person is abusive or threatening, follow your department's policy and tell your manager.

questions.prompt: Why should you acknowledge a complaint straight away?

options.text: The person knows it has arrived and when to expect a full reply
The acknowledgement counts as the final answer to the complaint
It removes the need for anyone to investigate the matter
It closes the case so no more letters are needed

questions.hint: Prompt acknowledgement reassures the person.

questions.prompt: A person raises four points in their complaint. What should your reply do?

options.text: Answer the two easiest points
Answer only the main point
Answer the points that were your fault
Answer every point they raised

questions.hint: A complete reply addresses each point.

questions.prompt: Which phrase sounds as if the problem is the person's feelings rather than the department's actions?

options.text: We regret that you feel let down
We are sorry we made an error
We have looked at your complaint
We will correct your record

questions.hint: Phrases such as 'that you feel' avoid owning the problem.

questions.prompt: The department made a mistake. Which sentence handles it best?

options.text: We regret any distress that may have been caused to you at this time.
Your claim was closed in error by the computer system last month.
Mistakes can happen in any large organisation, as you will understand.
We made a mistake when we closed your claim. I am sorry, and I have reopened it today.

questions.hint: Plain ownership and action make the apology sincere.

questions.prompt: The department has not made a mistake. What is the best approach?

options.text: Say the complaint is not valid and end the letter there
Refer the person to the website without any explanation
Explain what happened and why, without being defensive
Apologise for everything so that the person calms down

questions.hint: Clear explanation shows respect.

questions.prompt: Who looks into complaints about government departments when someone is still unhappy after the department's process, usually via an MP?

options.text: The Cabinet Office press team and its communications staff
The Information Commissioner's Office and its casework team
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
The National Audit Office and its financial auditors

questions.hint: The PHSO is the final stage for complaints about government bodies.

questions.prompt: What should you tell a person who is still unhappy after your reply?

options.text: That they must pay a fee before they can make an appeal
That their complaint will be ignored if they write again
That the matter is now closed and they cannot ask again
What they can do next, such as the next stage of the complaints process

questions.hint: People should know their options.

questions.prompt: Why keep a clear record of a complaint and your reply?

options.text: It shows what was said and done if the case goes further
It allows the person who made the error to be blamed
It removes the need to answer the person who complained
It means the complaint can be reopened without checking

questions.hint: Records support fairness and review.

items.title: Spreadsheets: VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP basics (Level 4)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Lookup functions find a value in a table. VLOOKUP looks for a value in the first column of a range and returns a value from another column in the same row. Its form is =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_range, column_number, FALSE). The column number counts from the first column of the range, so 1 is the lookup column itself. The last argument matters: FALSE (or 0) asks for an exact match, while TRUE (or leaving it out) asks for an approximate match, which only works properly on data sorted in ascending order. For most office tasks use FALSE. Suppose A2:C5 holds 101 Ali Finance; 102 Beth HR; 103 Chen IT; 104 Dana HR, in columns for ID, Name and Department. Then =VLOOKUP(103,A2:C5,2,FALSE) returns Chen, and =VLOOKUP(103,A2:C5,3,FALSE) returns IT. If the ID is not in the table, as in =VLOOKUP(105,A2:C5,2,FALSE), the result is the error #N/A. VLOOKUP can only look to the right of the lookup column, so you cannot use it to find an ID from a name unless the ID column moves. XLOOKUP is a newer function in Excel 2021, Microsoft 365 and Google Sheets. Its form is =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_range, return_range, [if_not_found]). It defaults to an exact match, can look to the left, and lets you choose what to show if no match is found, for example =XLOOKUP(105,A2:A5,B2:B5,"Not found") returns Not found. Check that the lookup values are the same type. The number 103 stored as text will not match the number 103.

questions.prompt: Using the table A2:C5 (101 Ali Finance, 102 Beth HR, 103 Chen IT, 104 Dana HR), what does =VLOOKUP(103,A2:C5,2,FALSE) return?

options.text: IT
Chen
#N/A

questions.hint: Column 2 of the row for 103 is the name.

questions.prompt: With the same table, what does =VLOOKUP(103,A2:C5,3,FALSE) return?

options.text: HR
Chen
IT

questions.hint: Column 3 holds the department.

questions.prompt: If the ID searched for is 105, which is not in the table, what result does VLOOKUP give?

options.text: #N/A
#REF!
Blank

questions.hint: A missing exact match returns #N/A.

questions.prompt: In VLOOKUP, what does the last argument FALSE ask for?

options.text: An exact match
A match in the last column
An approximate match
A match in sorted data only

questions.hint: FALSE means exact match.

questions.prompt: In =VLOOKUP(103,A2:C5,3,FALSE), what does the 3 refer to?

options.text: The number of matches that the function will return
The third row of the table range being searched
The third column of the table range
The value 3 which is being looked up in the table

questions.hint: The column number counts from the first column of the range.

questions.prompt: With the same table, what does =XLOOKUP(105,A2:A5,B2:B5,"Not found") return?

options.text: Blank
Not found
#N/A

questions.hint: The fourth argument is used when no match exists.

questions.prompt: Why might =VLOOKUP(103,...) fail when 103 appears in the table?

options.text: The 103 in the table may be stored as text, not a number
VLOOKUP cannot find numbers with three digits in them
The table range is too short to contain the number
The formula has been typed into column D by mistake

questions.hint: A number stored as text does not match a real number.

questions.prompt: Which function is available in Excel 2021, Microsoft 365 and Google Sheets and defaults to an exact match?

options.text: VLOOKUP
SUMIF
COUNTIF
XLOOKUP

questions.hint: XLOOKUP is the newer lookup function with exact matching by default.

items.title: Spreadsheets: combining functions and calculating proportions (Level 4)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Functions can be placed inside each other. The inner part is worked out first. For example =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B6),1) first finds the average and then rounds it to one decimal place. Suppose B2:B6 holds sales of 120, 80, 200, 50 and 150. The total is 600 and the average is 120. =IF(SUM(B2:B6)>500,"Over","Within") returns Over, because 600 is greater than 500. To find what share of the total one item represents, divide it by the total and format the result as a percentage: =B4/SUM($B$2:$B$6) returns one third for the 200, shown as 33.3% with one decimal place. Percentages of a total should add to 100%. Other common calculations are a discount, for example 15% off £80 is =80*(1-15%), which gives £68, and getting the price before VAT, for example =120/1.2, which gives 100. Do not add 20% back on to a VAT-inclusive price to take VAT off, because 120 minus 20% is 96, not 100. A weekly total might be =7.5*5, giving 37.5 hours. Beware averaging averages. If one team of 2 averages 10 and another of 8 averages 20, the overall average is not 15. It is (2*10 + 8*20)/10 = 18. Write formulas that refer to cells, not typed numbers, so that they update. Check results with a quick mental estimate to see if the answer is sensible.

questions.prompt: B2:B6 holds 120, 80, 200, 50 and 150. What does =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B6),1) return?
questions.hint: The average is exactly 120, so rounding changes nothing.

questions.prompt: With the same sales figures, what does =IF(SUM(B2:B6)>500,"Over","Within") return?

options.text: TRUE
Within
Over

questions.hint: The total of 600 is greater than 500.

questions.prompt: With the same figures, what share of the total does the 200 represent?
questions.hint: 200 divided by 600 is one third.

questions.prompt: Why does the formula for a share of the total often use $B$2:$B$6?

options.text: So that the formula cannot be deleted by anyone else
So the numbers in the formula are shown in dollars
So that the formula ignores the largest value in the range
So the total range stays fixed when the formula is copied down

questions.hint: Absolute references keep the denominator fixed.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives 15% off a price of £80?
questions.hint: Multiplying by 85% gives the discounted price.

questions.prompt: A price including 20% VAT is £120. What is the price before VAT?
questions.hint: 120 divided by 1.2 is 100.

questions.prompt: A team of 2 averages 10 and a team of 8 averages 20. What is the overall average?
A worker does 7.5 hours a day for 5 days. Which formula gives the weekly hours?

options.text: =7.5/5 giving 1.5

questions.hint: Hours are multiplied by days.

items.title: Spreadsheets: errors and checking your results (Level 4)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Spreadsheet errors can mislead whole teams, so checking is part of the job. Excel shows error codes that tell you what is wrong. #DIV/0! means a division by zero or an empty cell. #N/A means a value cannot be found, which is common in lookups. #NAME? means Excel does not recognise something in the formula, often a misspelt function name such as =SUMM(A1:A3). #REF! means a reference is no longer valid, usually because a cell, row or column it pointed to was deleted. #VALUE! means the formula has a value of the wrong type, such as adding text to a number. #### simply means the column is too narrow. A circular reference occurs when a formula refers to its own cell, for example typing =A1+A2 into A2. Excel warns you. Not every error shows a code. Many are silent. A SUM may leave out a number stored as text, a range may miss the last row, or a total may include a row that should be excluded. Good checking habits include: do a quick estimate to see if the result looks sensible, compare the total with another source, add a check cell that confirms sub-totals equal the grand total, and avoid typing numbers inside formulas, because they are easy to forget when something changes. Keep one version of the file and use clear labels and units. Hidden rows are still included in SUM, though SUBTOTAL can be used to leave out rows hidden by a filter. Do not rely on colour alone to mark something. Protect cells with formulas, so they are not overwritten by accident.

questions.prompt: Which error appears when you type =SUMM(A1:A3)?

options.text: #REF!
#N/A
#NAME?
#DIV/0!

questions.hint: Excel does not recognise the misspelt function name.

questions.prompt: Which error appears when a formula refers to a cell that has been deleted?

options.text: #NAME?
#REF!
#N/A
#VALUE!

questions.hint: #REF! means the reference is no longer valid.

questions.prompt: Which error is typical when VLOOKUP cannot find the value it is looking for?

options.text: #VALUE!
#DIV/0!
#N/A

questions.hint: #N/A means the value is not available.

questions.prompt: What causes #VALUE! in a formula like =A1+A2?

options.text: A1 and A2 are in different columns of the sheet
A cell holds text that cannot be added
The formula has been copied from another sheet
The column is too narrow to show the answer

questions.hint: Using text where a number is needed causes #VALUE!.

questions.prompt: What is a circular reference?

options.text: A chart that shows the data as a circular pie
A formula that repeats the same function several times
A cell that has been formatted with a circular border
A formula that refers to its own cell

questions.hint: A formula cannot depend on its own result.

questions.prompt: A SUM total looks too low. Which cause is plausible?

options.text: The column headings are in bold
The sheet has too many columns
Some numbers are stored as text
The font is too small

questions.hint: Text numbers are ignored by SUM.

questions.prompt: Why is a check cell useful?

options.text: It makes the whole sheet look tidier on the screen
It hides all of the formulas from other people
It confirms that sub-totals equal the grand total
It protects the sheet so that nobody can edit it

questions.hint: Check cells spot mistakes.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to type a VAT rate such as 1.2 directly into many formulas?

options.text: It is easy to miss one when the rate changes; a rate cell is safer
Formulas cannot hold numbers typed directly inside them
It makes the sheet file larger and slower to open
The rate cannot be formatted as a percentage there

questions.hint: A single input cell makes updates easy.

questions.prompt: What does SUBTOTAL allow you to do that SUM does not?

options.text: Ignore every negative number in the range
Leave out rows hidden by a filter
Add numbers that are stored as text
Add together cells that contain only text

questions.hint: SUBTOTAL can ignore filtered-out rows.

questions.prompt: You hide row 5 manually and use SUM. What happens to the value in row 5?

options.text: It is replaced by zero in the cell itself
It is still included in the total
It is removed from the total as soon as it is hidden
It turns into text when the row is hidden

questions.hint: SUM includes hidden rows.

items.title: Spreadsheets: tidying text, dates and summarising data (Level 4)
items.source: Microsoft Excel help; Google Sheets help
items.body: Real data is often messy, and a few text functions can clean it. TRIM removes extra spaces from the start and end of text and between words, so ' Smith ' becomes 'Smith'. UPPER changes text to capitals, LOWER to lower case and PROPER to capital letters at the start of each word. LEN counts the characters in a cell. LEFT and RIGHT take a number of characters from the start or end, so =LEFT("AB123",2) returns AB. The ampersand joins text: =A2&" "&B2 joins a first and last name with a space between. CONCAT and TEXTJOIN do a similar job. Dates are stored as numbers, so you can subtract them: if A2 holds 1 March 2025 and B2 holds 31 March 2025, =B2-A2 returns 30. TODAY() returns the current date and changes each day. A pivot table summarises a large table by category without writing formulas. For example, it can show the total amount for each department. To create one, select the data, which should have clear headings and no blank rows, and choose Insert then PivotTable. If you change the original data you must refresh the pivot table. Conditional formatting changes how cells look when a rule is met, for example showing overdue dates in red. It does not change values. Data should be kept in a tidy table of one record per row. Avoid putting notes or totals in the middle of the data and avoid merged cells.

questions.prompt: Which function removes extra spaces from the start, end and middle of text?

options.text: PROPER
CLEAN
TRIM
LEN

questions.hint: TRIM removes the extra spaces.

questions.prompt: What does =LEFT("AB123",2) return?

options.text: B1
A
AB

questions.hint: LEFT takes the first two characters.

questions.prompt: Which formula joins a first name in A2 and a last name in B2 with a space between?

options.text: =A2*B2 with a space typed in
=A2,B2 with a comma in the middle
=A2+B2 with a space typed in

questions.hint: The ampersand joins text.

questions.prompt: A2 holds 1 March 2025 and B2 holds 31 March 2025. What does =B2-A2 return?
questions.hint: Subtracting dates gives the number of days between them.

questions.prompt: What does TODAY() return?

options.text: A fixed date that was saved in the file
The date on which the file was first created
The current date, which changes each day
The date on which the file was last edited

questions.hint: TODAY updates when the file is opened.

questions.prompt: What is a pivot table used for?

options.text: Splitting a workbook into two separate workbooks
Summarising a large table by category without writing formulas
Locking cells to stop other people editing them
Checking spelling and grammar in a table

questions.hint: Pivot tables summarise data.

questions.prompt: What must you do after changing the source data of a pivot table?

options.text: Delete and rebuild the sheet
Sort the original table again
Save the workbook as a CSV
Refresh the pivot table

questions.hint: Pivot tables update when refreshed.

questions.prompt: Which layout is best for data that will be sorted and filtered?

options.text: Merged cells used for each department name
One record per row, with headings and no merged cells
Notes written in blank rows between the records
Totals inserted between groups of rows of records

questions.hint: Tidy tables sort and filter properly.

items.title: Security classifications: marking and handling decisions (Level 4)
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; HMG Security Policy Framework
items.body: The classification of a document should match the damage that its loss or compromise would cause, not how interesting it is. Over-classifying wastes effort and slows work, while under-classifying leaves information at risk. Most routine government work is OFFICIAL, and routine OFFICIAL information does not need a marking in every document. OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE is used where the information could have more damaging consequences if lost or published, such as personal data, commercially sensitive material or material about a policy not yet announced. Departments may add descriptors to show the kind of sensitivity, for example PERSONAL or COMMERCIAL. These descriptors are not classifications. Where you mark a document, put the marking at the top, and for SECRET and TOP SECRET at the top and bottom of every page. Email systems may apply a marking to the subject line or footer. When you share information, check the classification and the people who will receive it. OFFICIAL can be shared with partners who need it, using approved routes. SECRET and TOP SECRET can only be handled on approved systems and by cleared people, with stricter rules for storage, travel and destruction. Unmarked information is not automatically public. If you find a document that looks sensitive but has no marking, treat it with care and ask the owner. Information marked for the public, such as press releases once published, is not classified. If you are unsure which classification applies, ask the originator or the security team. Do not guess and do not reduce the classification yourself.

questions.prompt: On what should a document's classification be based?

options.text: The seniority of the person who wrote it
The harm that would follow if it were lost or disclosed
The number of people who have already read it
How interesting the contents are to other readers

questions.hint: Classification reflects the potential damage.

questions.prompt: What is a problem with over-classifying information?

options.text: It wastes effort and slows down work
It removes the need for handling rules
It reduces the need for cleared staff
It makes information too easy to share

questions.hint: Too high a classification adds unnecessary controls.

questions.prompt: Which of these would be most likely to need an OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE caveat?

options.text: A list of staff home addresses
A training schedule for next week
A published annual report
A list of public holidays

questions.hint: Personal data about staff could cause harm if released.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of descriptors such as PERSONAL and COMMERCIAL?

options.text: They apply only to information at the TOP SECRET level
They replace the classification when the information is shared
They create an extra level sitting between OFFICIAL and SECRET
They show the type of sensitivity, and are not extra classification levels

questions.hint: Descriptors explain the type of sensitivity; they are not levels.

questions.prompt: Where is the marking placed on SECRET and TOP SECRET documents?

options.text: On the first page of the document only
On the envelope used to post it only
At the top and bottom of every page
In the file name of the electronic copy

questions.hint: Higher classifications are marked on every page.

questions.prompt: You find an unmarked document that appears to hold sensitive details. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it with care and check with the owner
Delete it to be safe
Post it to the sender
Treat it as public because it has no marking

questions.hint: A lack of marking does not mean information is public.

questions.prompt: You think a document has been classified too highly. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the question because it is not your document
Lower the classification yourself, as you know best
Ask the originator or the security team
Remove the marking and send it on to the recipient

questions.hint: Only the owner changes a classification.

questions.prompt: Who can handle SECRET information?

options.text: Cleared people using approved systems
Any civil servant who works in the same team
Any government contractor who has signed a contract
Any manager of a grade high enough

questions.hint: SECRET needs both clearance and approved systems.

questions.prompt: Under what conditions can OFFICIAL information be shared with an external partner?

options.text: Whenever the partner has asked for it in writing
Where they need it and an approved route is used
Whenever it is sent to the partner by personal email
Never, because it must stay inside government at all times

questions.hint: OFFICIAL can be shared on a need-to-know basis through approved routes.

items.title: UK GDPR: rights, exceptions and special cases (Level 4)
items.source: ICO guidance on the UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: Some data protection rights have limits. The right to erasure, sometimes called the right to be forgotten, is not absolute. It does not apply where you must keep the data to meet a legal obligation or to perform a public task. The right to object lets a person challenge processing based on public task, though the organisation may continue if it has strong grounds. A person can ask for processing to be restricted while an accuracy complaint is checked. Data portability applies where processing is based on consent or a contract and is done by automated means. When a person asks to see their data in a subject access request, you do not give out other people's information. You may need to remove or redact third-party details. Organisations can refuse a request that is manifestly unfounded or excessive, but must explain why. Anonymised data, from which a person cannot be identified, is not personal data. Pseudonymised data, where names are replaced by codes but can be linked back, still is. Children's data needs particular care and privacy information should be written in language they can understand. The UK GDPR gives extra protection to decisions made solely by automated means that have a legal or similarly significant effect on someone, such as an automatic refusal of a benefit. A person can ask for human involvement. Personal data may be transferred outside the UK only if there are suitable protections in place, such as an adequacy decision or approved safeguards. A person can complain to the ICO if they think their rights have been breached, and can also take a claim to court.

questions.prompt: When does the right to erasure not apply?

options.text: When the person has asked in writing for erasure
When the data must be kept to meet a legal obligation
When the data is more than a year old now
When the person has changed their address recently

questions.hint: Legal obligations override the right to erasure.

questions.prompt: Which data is NOT personal data?

options.text: Truly anonymised data from which no one can be identified
A photograph of a person who can be identified
Pseudonymised data that can be linked back to a person
A list of names and addresses held in a database

questions.hint: Anonymised data falls outside the UK GDPR.

questions.prompt: What must you consider when answering a subject access request?

options.text: Whether the person has paid a standard fee first
Whether the person is a UK citizen or resident
Whether the data is more than 12 months old
Whether other people's details need to be removed

questions.hint: Requests must not reveal other people's data.

questions.prompt: Why does the UK GDPR give special protection to solely automated decisions with a significant effect?

options.text: Computers are not permitted to make any decisions
People can ask for a human to review them
Such decisions are always unlawful
Only senior staff may use such systems

questions.hint: A person can request human involvement.

questions.prompt: When can a request be refused as manifestly unfounded or excessive?

options.text: When it is clearly baseless or excessive, and the reasons are explained
When the department is very busy with other requests
When the person has made a complaint about it before
When the person has made a similar request at any time before

questions.hint: The refusal needs a clear justification.

questions.prompt: What does restricting processing allow?

options.text: Publishing the data in an anonymised form
Transferring the data to another organisation
Deleting the data immediately and for good
Pausing use of the data while its accuracy is checked

questions.hint: Restriction pauses processing.

questions.prompt: Why should privacy information written for children be in language they can understand?

options.text: Plain English is only ever suitable for children
Children's data is exempt from most of the rules
Children's data needs particular care and transparency
Children cannot have data protection rights of their own

questions.hint: Transparency must suit the audience.

questions.prompt: Where can a person complain if they think their data rights were breached?

options.text: To the ICO, and they can also go to court
To the National Audit Office, which audits accounts
To the police only, who then pass it on
To their local council only, as the local authority

questions.hint: The ICO handles complaints, and court claims are possible.

items.title: Social engineering and secure access (Level 4)
items.source: NCSC guidance on phishing and social engineering
items.body: Attackers do not only use email. Social engineering means tricking people into giving access or information. In pretexting, a caller invents a believable story, for example pretending to be from IT, a supplier or a senior manager. Vishing is phishing by phone, smishing by text, and quishing uses QR codes that lead to fake websites. Business email compromise is when an attacker pretends to be a manager or supplier to get a payment or bank details changed. Typical signs are urgency, secrecy and a request to bypass normal process, such as 'Don't tell anyone, I need this paid today'. The defence is to follow process whatever the pressure: check requests through a trusted route, make sure a second person approves payments or changes, and report anything odd. Multi-factor authentication can also be attacked. In MFA fatigue, an attacker repeatedly sends approval requests hoping the user will accept one by mistake. If you receive approval requests you did not start, do not approve them, and report it, because it may mean your password has been stolen. Password reset messages you did not ask for should be treated as a warning sign. Use a different password for each account, so one breach cannot unlock others. Keep software updated, because updates fix security flaws. Lock your screen. Never plug in unknown USB devices. When you leave an account open on a shared computer, others can use it, so always sign out. Tell your security team about suspicious calls, even if you did not fall for them, as the same caller may try others.

questions.prompt: In social engineering, what is pretexting?

options.text: Inventing a believable story to trick someone into giving access or information
Guessing a password again and again using software
Sending the same email to a very large number of people
Copying the design of a website to look genuine

questions.hint: Pretexting relies on a convincing false story.

questions.prompt: In cyber security, what is quishing?

options.text: Phishing carried out by telephone call
Phishing carried out by text message
Phishing that uses QR codes leading to fake websites
Phishing carried out through social media posts

questions.hint: Quishing uses QR codes.

questions.prompt: Which defence best reduces the risk of payment fraud?

options.text: A second person approves payments and bank detail changes
Trusting any email that includes the department logo
Using one strong password for all of your accounts
Paying faster whenever a senior manager asks you to

questions.hint: Controls such as dual approval stop single-person errors.

questions.prompt: You get several approval requests on your phone that you did not start. What should you do?

options.text: Do not approve them and report it, as your password may be stolen
Turn off MFA on the account to stop the requests
Approve one of them to make the requests stop
Ignore them completely and carry on working

questions.hint: Unexpected approval requests suggest an attacker has your password.

questions.prompt: Why should you tell the security team about a suspicious call even if you did not fall for it?

options.text: The same caller may try others
You may be disciplined otherwise
The caller may have your home address
The call can be recorded as a training example

questions.hint: Reports help to protect colleagues.

questions.prompt: Why do software updates matter for security?

options.text: They change your password to a stronger one
They make the computer run a good deal faster
They delete old files that are no longer needed
They fix security flaws that attackers can exploit

questions.hint: Updates close known vulnerabilities.

questions.prompt: Why should you sign out of an account on a shared computer?

options.text: To avoid having to pay for extra software licences
To save your files in the right folder for later
Otherwise the next user can use your account
To make the shared computer run a little faster

questions.hint: An open session gives others access.

questions.prompt: You receive an unexpected password reset email. What is the safest action?

options.text: Forward it to a friend who knows about computers
Reply to the sender to ask what the email is for
Do not follow the link; check your account through the normal route and report it
Follow the link to see what the message actually says

questions.hint: An unrequested reset can mean someone is trying to take over your account.

items.title: Sending information safely and handling breaches (Level 4)
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; NCSC guidance; HMG Security Policy Framework
items.body: Choosing the right way to send information is part of protecting it. Ask what is being sent, how sensitive it is, who needs it and what the safest approved method is. Email is suitable for much OFFICIAL information inside government because government systems use secure connections, but sending personal or sensitive data outside government by ordinary email carries risks. Use approved secure file sharing or encryption, and send access details separately. Do not use personal email, personal cloud storage or consumer messaging apps for work. Check the address, especially for people with similar names, and consider turning off auto-complete or checking the full address. Send the minimum: attach only the file needed, remove hidden data and personal data not required, and consider sending a summary instead of the full record. When posting paper, check the address, use the right envelope and use tracked delivery for sensitive material. When you realise there has been a breach, act at once: stop the incident if you can, for example by trying to recall the email, tell your manager and the data protection team, and write down what happened while it is fresh. Do not ask the wrong recipient to delete the information without guidance, and do not contact affected people yourself unless told to. The team will decide whether the ICO and the individuals must be told. Learning matters more than blame: reports help the department fix the cause, such as removing risky features. Reporting promptly, honestly and fully is always better than hoping the matter goes unnoticed.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in choosing how to send information?

options.text: Pick whichever method is the quickest available
Use whichever method you used the last time
Ask the recipient to choose the method they prefer
Consider how sensitive it is and who needs it

questions.hint: The sensitivity and audience determine the safe method.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT an approved way to share official information?

options.text: A personal cloud storage account
A department-approved file sharing service
A secure government messaging service
An encrypted attachment with the password sent separately

questions.hint: Personal accounts are outside the department's control.

questions.prompt: Why attach only the file that is needed?

options.text: Email systems reject any extra attachments sent
It follows the data minimisation principle and limits harm if it goes wrong
It saves paper when the email is printed out
It makes the email shorter and quicker to read

questions.hint: Sharing the minimum reduces risk.

questions.prompt: Which step is best for posting sensitive paper documents?

options.text: Check the address and use tracked delivery
Post them with ordinary stamps in the usual way
Leave them with a neighbour if nobody is in
Use a reused envelope to save on costs

questions.hint: Tracking shows the item arrived.

questions.prompt: You realise you emailed a customer's details to the wrong person. What should you do first?

options.text: Ask the recipient to delete it without telling anyone else
Try to recall the email, then tell your manager and the data protection team straight away
Wait to see whether the recipient replies to the email
Contact the customer yourself to explain what happened

questions.hint: Act at once and report so that the team can decide what to do.

questions.prompt: Why write down what happened while it is fresh?

options.text: It is only needed for the largest of breaches
It replaces the need to report the breach at all
It helps the team assess the breach accurately
It lets you decide who ought to take the blame

questions.hint: Accurate details help the response.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether the ICO and affected individuals must be told?

options.text: The data protection team, using the organisation's procedures
The customer whose details were sent in error
The person who made the mistake in the first place
The recipient of the email, once they have read it

questions.hint: The organisation's data protection team assesses risk.

questions.prompt: What attitude to breach reporting does the Civil Service encourage?

options.text: Waiting to see whether the problem goes away by itself
Prompt, honest reporting so lessons can be learnt
Reporting only when someone outside makes a complaint
Blaming the individual who made the error in public

questions.hint: Open reporting helps the department fix causes.
